newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Chretien in tight race in home riding.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Chretien in tight race in home riding.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien is in a tight race with separatist Bloc Quebecois candidate Yves Duhaime in Chretien's Saint-Maurice riding, according to a SOM poll published on Thursday in Le Soleil.

After redistribution of the 25 percent of respondents who were undecided, Chretien would get 46 percent of the vote in the Quebec riding, while Duhaime would get 45 percent, the Quebec City French-language daily newspaper said.
The poll of 661 voters was taken April 25 to 27 and had a margin of error of four percent, 19 times out of 20.

In the 1993 federal election, some polls showed Chretien in trouble in Saint-Maurice riding about 175 km (108.7 miles) northeast of Montreal, which he has held for most of the past 34 years. Chretien ended up winning by about 6,400 votes.
Chretien's challenger in the riding, which includes his hometown of Shawinigan, represented the riding for the Parti Quebecois in the provincial National Assembly from 1976 to 1985.
Duhaime recently lost the leadership of the Bloc Quebecois to Gilles Duceppe in a hard-fought contest that revealed divisions in the separatist party.

In an analysis accompanying the SOM poll, Le Soleil columnist Michel Vastel wrote that Chretien would likely win his riding, but probably would have lost if Duhaime had won the Bloc Quebecois leadership.
Meanwhile, the SOM poll showed Conservative leader Jean Charest and New Democratic Party leader Alexa McDonough with solid leads over their rivals in their home ridings.
After redistribution of the 25 percent undecided vote, the survey had Charest leading with 60 percent in Sherbrooke riding in Quebec's Eastern Townships region.
Bloc Quebecois candidate Jacques Blanchette had 26 percent, while Liberal Martin Bureau had 11 percent.

In her Halifax riding, NDP leader McDonough led Liberal incumbent Mary Clancy by 43 percent to 31 percent, with 16 percent for the Conservative candidate, the SOM polled showed. The undecided vote was 24 percent.
The Halifax poll was taken April 25 to 29 and like the Saint-Maurice and Sherbrooke surveys, polled 660 voters and had a margin of error of four percent, 19 times out of 20.
